Arrow keys move the selected object left, right, forward and back; Page Up and Page Down move it up and down. With nothing selected, the arrow keys turn the view. Plus and minus zoom. Keys 1 to 4 pick a view: front, side, top, corner. The Scene list in the Inspector lets you pick objects from the keyboard, and the Inspector's number boxes set exact positions, turns and sizes. Tab edits the points of the selected object (Tab again, or Escape with no points picked, goes back); Shift+Tab or F6 leaves the 3D view.

    Settings

    While Snap is on (the magnet in the top bar), dragging moves and turns in these steps, and resizing keeps sizes to whole move steps. The arrow keys always move by the move step (Shift for ten times as far). Hold Alt (Option) while dragging to move freely.

    The mood a new scene starts with. Each scene keeps its own lighting, saved with it.

    The Resize tool's handles grow an object towards the handle, and the opposite side stays put. Off: it grows from its middle, both ways.

    On: a model you open keeps the positions saved in its file. Off: it lands on the floor in the middle of the view.

    Keys without Ctrl, such as W for Move or 1 for the front view. Turn them off if they get in the way of speech input or another tool. Shortcuts with Ctrl, the arrow keys and Delete keep working.

    Draw the outline

    Start from:

    Click to add a point (click on a line to add it there). Drag a point to move it. Double-click a point (or use the Smooth button) to make it smooth (round dot) or a sharp corner (square). Keys: [ and ] pick a point, arrows move it (Shift: 5 times as far), Insert adds a point after it, Delete removes it, S makes it smooth or sharp, + and - zoom, F fits the view round the outline, Ctrl+Enter uses the outline. To round a sharp corner (a true circle, not a smooth point that thins the wall), type its radius in the list's Round box.

    Tutorials

    Each one is a few short steps with a picture. A small panel shows the steps beside the 3D view, so you can follow along. It remembers your step.

      Picture

      3DEDTR

      On a Mac, Ctrl means Cmd. Single keys can be turned off in Settings.

      3DEDTR builds models out of simple shapes, the way you would with building blocks or clay.

      1. Add a shape with the shape buttons on the tool rail (down the left, or along the bottom on a phone or tablet). It lands on the grid, in the middle of the view.
      2. Look around. Drag an empty part of the view to turn around the model. To slide the view, hold Space and drag, right-drag with a mouse, or drag with two fingers on a touch screen; to zoom, scroll or pinch. The Front, Side, Top and Corner buttons jump to a standard view.
      3. Move, turn (rotate) and resize with the Move (W), Turn (E) and Resize (R) tools: drag the coloured arrows, rings or handles. Red is X (left and right), green is Y (up and down), blue is Z (towards you and away). For exact numbers, type them into the Inspector.
      4. Merge shapes. Pick two or more that overlap (Shift+click, or Pick several on a touch screen), then choose Union, Subtract or Intersect in the Inspector.
      5. Make it move. The film button (or T) shows the timeline. Pick an object and press Add keyframe; move the play head, change the object, and add another keyframe. Play glides it from one to the next. Ready-made... adds a turntable, reveal, exploded view, cross-fade or camera move in one go; with nothing picked, Add keyframe remembers the view. Export, then Video, makes an MP4 or WebM of it.
      6. Words and outlines. The Text button (the T icon on the tool rail) adds 3D letters: type in the Inspector, pick a typeface (Inter, Noto Serif, Zilla Slab, Atkinson Hyperlegible for easy reading, Nunito, Anton, Pacifico, or a Stencil whose letters stay in one piece when cut through a plate), set the letter height and depth. The star button adds an extruded shape: a star, heart, arrow, polygon, rounded rectangle, ring or cross - or pick "Draw your own" as its Outline and draw one. Both are solids like any other: make text a hole to engrave it.
      7. Holes. Set an object's Kind to Hole: it turns see-through, and any merge cuts it out of the solids. Handy for screw holes and slots. Quicker still: Hole through a face (D), then click a face, puts a round hole right through it.
      8. Drawings. Open an SVG (from VCTREDTR or any drawing app) and it becomes a solid you can set the depth of, holes and all.
      9. Lights. The bulb button adds a spot light aimed at the model. Change it to a bulb or a sun, pick its colour and brightness, and turn it to aim it. Lights can move and fade in an animation. Scene settings has moods too: Product, Dramatic, Sunset.
      10. Ready to print? Lay flat (L) turns an object onto its biggest flat face, and Export, STL makes the file for your slicer.
      11. Group parts that belong together (Ctrl+G): they move as one and keep their own colours. Click a group once to pick it, and again to pick one part. Join into one solid merges a group, cutting out its holes.
      12. Place things exactly. With two or more picked, Put next to makes a row or a stack with a gap. Put on a face (P) puts the selection against a face you click. The Measure tool (M) measures between two points.
      13. Name things in the Inspector's Name box, or double-click a row in the Scene list (F2 from the keyboard).
      14. Made a mistake? Undo (Ctrl+Z, or the curved arrow in the top bar) takes back the last change, as many times as you need. Redo is Ctrl+Shift+Z.
      15. Save your project with the disk button (Ctrl+Shift+S) and give it a name. You get a .3dedtr file that keeps everything editable. Next time, open it with the folder button (Ctrl+O) and carry on.
      16. Export. STL goes to a 3D printer's slicer. OBJ and GLB open in other 3D apps (GLB keeps the colours). PNG makes a picture.

      On a phone or tablet, the Inspector button in the top-right corner opens the Scene list and the settings of what you picked. Drag the handle at the top of the Inspector up or down to give it (or the 3D view) more room; tap the handle to open or close it.

      Merge Shapes

      The first object you pick is the one that is kept: the result takes its colour, and Subtract cuts the others out of it. Little numbers in the Scene list show the order.

        Sizes and 3D printing

        One grid square is 10 mm, and every number in the Inspector is in millimetres, the unit slicers use. 3DEDTR's up is Y (like most 3D apps); STL export turns the model so Z is up, which is what printers expect. Use Drop to the floor so a model sits flat on the print bed.

        3DEDTR is a 3D modeling app. Build models from basic shapes, group them, cut holes, merge them with Union, Subtract and Intersect, and export them for 3D printing (STL), for other 3D apps (OBJ, GLB) or as a picture (PNG).

        Private by design. Your models never leave this device. There are no uploads, accounts or analytics, and the page's security policy blocks it from sending data anywhere.

        The 3D engine is three.js r186 (three.js authors), with three-mesh-bvh 0.9.15 and three-bvh-csg 0.0.18 by Garrett Johnson for Merge Shapes. All three are MIT licensed. They ship with the app in its engine folder (licences in engine/LICENSES.txt), so no outside server supplies any of the code this page runs.

        Projects. Save project keeps everything editable in a .3dedtr file. Export makes an STL, OBJ, GLB or PNG for other apps.

        Part of a family of browser tools that all work this way - see More apps.
